# Results — Study 627 (13F Cloning)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The claim under test — **copy
Berkshire Hathaway's 13F 45 days late and you still beat the market**, the free-rider trade
that supposedly should not work but does — rebuilt literally: every original 13F-HR Berkshire
filed on EDGAR since the XML era (periods 2013-06-30 → 2026-03-31), top-10 holdings by
reported value, rebalanced at the close of the **first trading day after each filing date**
(the 45-day disclosure lag is *inside* the filing date), equal-weight and value-weight, raced
against SPY and against Berkshire itself on total-return prices. Offline & deterministic once
cached; run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number. As-of **2026-06-30** (the
last complete calendar month). Fingerprint `ddad544e0e75`.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Filings | **52** original 13F-HR (CIK 0001067983), periods 2013-06-30 → 2026-03-31, filed 2013-08-15 → 2026-05-15; amendments (13F-HR/A) excluded — the clone only sees what was public on the filing date |
| Universe | **30** distinct CUSIPs ever in the top 10, mapped by a hardcoded CUSIP→ticker table; **28** priceable on yfinance |
| Slot coverage | **507/520** top-10 slots priced (**97.5%**) — the 13 missing slots are DIRECTV and Activision Blizzard (acquired & delisted, no surviving tape; weights renormalised) |
| Prices | yfinance daily **auto-adjusted (total-return)** closes, 2013-01-02 → 2026-06-30 (3,393 days) for the 28 names + **SPY** + **BRK-B** + **^IRX** (risk-free leg) |
| Race window | **2013-09-30 → 2026-06-30** — **154** complete months (12.8 years) |
| Execution / costs | exactly **one** lag: rebalance at the close of the first trading day **after** the filing date; costs **one-way bps × traded NAV** at each rebalance (EW one-way turnover 10.0%/rebalance ≈ 40%/yr) |

> **Survivorship & window (named on the Signal axis).** Two acquired-and-delisted names
> (DIRECTV 2015, Activision 2023) have no yfinance tape: 2.5% of top-10 slots are dropped and
> renormalised — both were pinned merger targets at the time, so the omission is small in
> either direction. Bigger and more honest: the test window is the **post-2013 XML era only**
> (that is when machine-readable 13F filings begin), a mega-cap growth bull market in which
> value-tilted Berkshire itself lagged the index. The folk claim's supporting studies live on
> **1976–2006** tape; this study answers what cloning did **since you could actually script
> it** — and cannot rule on the earlier era.

## The race — clone (filing date + 1) vs SPY, monthly, 154 months

| leg | clone CAGR | SPY CAGR | active (ann.) | HAC *t* (NW lags 4) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **EW gross** | **8.78%** | 14.51% | **−4.86%/yr** | **−2.11** |
| EW net @ 10 bps one-way | 8.70% | 14.51% | −4.94%/yr | −2.14 |
| **VW gross** | **11.52%** | 14.51% | **−2.27%/yr** | −1.07 |
| VW net @ 10 bps one-way | 11.46% | 14.51% | −2.32%/yr | −1.09 |

CAPM on monthly **excess-vs-excess** returns (^IRX risk-free): EW gross alpha
**−4.43%/yr** (HAC *t* = −1.72) at beta **0.97**; VW gross alpha **−2.62%/yr**
(HAC *t* = −1.24) at beta **1.03**. Sharpe (excess) **0.49** (EW) / **0.62** (VW) vs SPY
**0.89**. Max drawdown: clone EW **−30.7%**, VW **−26.3%**, SPY **−23.9%**.

The folk claim is **inverted** on this tape: the 45-day-late Berkshire clone did not beat the
market — the equal-weight clone underperformed SPY by **−4.86%/yr** with a *significantly
negative* HAC *t* of **−2.11**, and the value-weight clone (carried by its giant AAPL slug)
still lost −2.27%/yr. There is no positive signal anywhere on the tape.

## Costs are NOT the problem

EW one-way turnover is **10.0% per rebalance** (~40%/yr): at 10 bps one-way the total cost
drag is **8.7 bps/yr** — three orders of magnitude smaller than the −486 bps/yr shortfall.
The clone is one of the cheapest, most accessible trades imaginable (ten mega-caps, four
trades a year). It fails on signal, not friction.

| slice | active (ann.) | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|

| 2020–2026 (78 m) | −5.86%/yr | −1.41 |
| top-5 clone (EW) | −3.39%/yr | −1.36 |
| **top-10 clone (EW, headline)** | **−4.86%/yr** | **−2.11** |
| top-15 clone (EW) | −3.56%/yr | −1.64 |

The shortfall is not one bad half-decade and not an artefact of where the top-N line is
drawn: every slice and every N is negative.

## Random-manager placebo — Berkshire's ranking was worse than chance

200 random managers (seed 627 — averaged over ≥ 20 seeds per the house rule) pick 10 names
at random from the **same 28-name universe** on the **same filing calendar with the same
lag**, equal-weight:

| quantity | value |
|---|--:|
| random managers' mean active vs SPY | **+0.26%/yr** (sd 1.53) |
| random managers' mean CAGR | 14.33% |
| actual EW clone active | −4.86%/yr — **−3.34 sd** below the random mean |
| share of random managers as bad or worse | **0.0%** |

Holding *Berkshire-flavoured mega-caps* roughly matched the index. Berkshire's actual
**top-10 ranking** — the thing the clone free-rides on — underperformed **all 200** random
selections from its own universe. The 45-day lag isn't the killer; the picks were.

## Third axis — does the clone at least beat Berkshire itself? (the cash-drag story)

The clone free-rides Berkshire's *fully-invested* stock sleeve while Berkshire the company
drags a giant cash pile — so the clone "should" beat BRK. It doesn't:

| leg | clone CAGR | BRK-B CAGR | active | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| EW clone vs BRK-B | 8.78%/yr | 12.43%/yr | **−3.40%/yr** | −1.16 |
| VW clone vs BRK-B | 11.52%/yr | 12.43%/yr | **−0.81%/yr** | −0.23 |

Berkshire the *company* (operating businesses + cash optionality, itself 2.1 pp/yr behind
SPY here) beat its own cloneable 13F sleeve. The cash-drag free-ride is **busted** — you
were better off buying BRK-B than photocopying its stock picks, and better off with SPY than
either.

## Synthetic control — the machinery is faithful

A deterministic monthly world where a manager with **planted** skill discloses through
quarterly filings read with a 45-day lag (exactly the clone's information set):

| planted manager alpha | clone active vs market | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|
| **0%/yr (null)** | −1.13%/yr | **−0.76** |
| **+8%/yr** | +5.07%/yr | **+3.39** |

With no skill the clone harness does not manufacture significance; with planted skill it
recovers ~2/3 of the alpha (the lag + quarterly-rotation haircut) and clears *t* ≥ 2. So the
real-tape −4.86%/yr at *t* = −2.11 is a genuine measurement, not a construction artefact —
and the haircut also says a skilled manager's clone *could* have shown up on this harness.
*(Machinery proof only — never cited as market evidence.)*

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** The claim is that the lagged clone *beats the market*. On 154 months of
  post-2013 tape it did the opposite: EW active **−4.86%/yr (HAC t = −2.11)**, VW
  **−2.27%/yr (t = −1.07)**, negative in both halves and at top-5/10/15, and **below all 200
  random managers** drawn from its own universe. Survivorship (97.5% slot coverage, two
  delisted acquirees) and the post-2013-only window are named — the pre-2013 literature era
  is out of scope, but on every month you could actually script it, the free ride went
  backwards.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** Access is perfect (ten mega-caps, four trades/yr, ~40%/yr
  one-way turnover, **8.7 bps/yr** drag at 10 bps) — and there is nothing to harvest. Costs
  are not the problem; the signal is. A perfectly tradable way to lag the index.
- **"Beats Berkshire itself (cash drag)?" — BUSTED.** The fully-invested clone lost to
  BRK-B too (EW −3.40%/yr, VW −0.81%/yr). Berkshire's cash-dragging whole beat its
  cloneable parts.
